There is one small change that makes a disagreement easier to have, and it is not about being polite. It is about the tense. Compare two sentences. The first one is: that policy is wrong. The second one is: if it were my decision, I would start somewhere else. Both say the same thing, and the second one is far easier to answer, because it puts the idea one step away from the person saying it. The other side can argue with the idea without arguing with you. This is why so much of the language of negotiation and of public argument sits in the hypothetical. It is not weakness and it is not indirectness for its own sake. It is a way of keeping a conversation open long enough for somebody to change their mind, including you.

The most useful question I have ever learned in a professional argument is six words long. What would change your mind here. Not why do you think that, which people hear as an attack, and not are you sure, which they hear as doubt about them. What would change your mind. It asks for the shape of their thinking, not for a defence of their conclusion, and almost nobody has ever been asked it. Two things happen when you do. The first is that they slow down, because they have to think instead of repeat. The second is the one that matters. Sooner or later somebody asks you the same question back, and you find out whether you have an answer. If nothing would change your mind, then what you have is not an opinion. It is a position, and those are much less interesting to talk about.
